extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, philosophers of mathematics, and graduate students interested in the methodology of mathematical proof and theory-change
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts methodological standards for producing and assessing mathematical proofs, conjectures, counterexamples, and concept-change (proofs-and-refutations style). Focuses on heuristics such as concept-stretching, monster-barring, test severity, and theoretical versus naive classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for proof-generated (theoretical) concepts over naive concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Naive concepts (e.g. the crystal-like 'polyhedron' with plane faces) are often superseded by proof-generated or theoretical concepts produced by proofs and refutations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing concepts, prefer those that arise from proofs and explanations (proof-generated concepts such as 'Cauchy-objects' or projectability/stretchability notions) rather than clinging to naive pre-theoretical meanings. Example: the naive meaning of 'polyhedron' disappears when replaced by proof-generated concepts referring to stretchability, pumpability, photographability, projectability, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory-generated classification should replace naive/taxonomical classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifications grounded in theoretical explanations (proof-generated classifications) are epistemically superior to naive or nominal classifications based only on superficial features or names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate classifications by their explanatory power and how they arise from proofs; e.g. replace naive categories like 'cavity' or 'tunnel' with theoretical notions like multiply-connectedness when the theory of surfaces/topology provides better explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic versus logical counterexamples (and their treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterexamples that appear in practice are fundamentally heuristic; 'logical' counterexamples typically arise only after changing the language or stretching concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a counterexample appears, decide whether to (a) refuse it within the original language (keep tacit semantic rules) or (b) change the language by concept-stretching and accept it as a counterexample in the new language. Recognize that logical counterexamples are often created by altering definitions or rules of discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish naive counterexamples ('freaks') from theoretical counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Naive counterexamples (freaks) arise from arbitrary or accidental concept-stretchings and may be unexplained anomalies; theoretical counterexamples are produced or explained by extended proofs/theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat freaks with suspicion: they may be mistakes or instances of a different theory. Attempt to convert freaks into theoretical counterexamples by expanding or deepening proofs; only when that fails consider theory-revision or abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept-stretching is a legitimate methodological move but must be demarcated
rubrics_metrics.description: Concept-stretching (expanding the meaning of terms) is a common source of refutation and discovery, but if unrestricted it destroys meaning and truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish rational (slight, well-motivated) stretching from irrational, surreptitious or arbitrary stretching. Develop criteria for acceptable stretches so that refutational practice remains disciplined rather than arbitrary reinterpretation that trivializes truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of unlimited concept-stretching (destroys meaning/truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any proposition one can find sufficiently narrow or sufficiently wide interpretations that make it true or false; unlimited stretching will leave no true statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid allowing arbitrary reinterpretations of constituents of propositions. If one accepts every possible stretching as legitimate refutation, mathematical truth degenerates into vacuous refutability; conversely, absolute fixation on a single linguistic form forces monster-barring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monster-barring and monster-adjustment are ad hoc and problematic
rubrics_metrics.description: Monster-barring (adding clauses to exclude refuting 'monsters') and monster-adjustment are tactics to protect theorems from refutation by redefining terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use monster-barring only cautiously: it risks an infinite regress of clauses and can become mere linguistic therapy rather than advancing understanding. Prefer theoretical explanation or deeper proofs over ad hoc exclusion clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity of tests (simple vs severe) — tests can generate proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests of conjectures range from 'simple' to 'severe'; severe tests may produce the first hints of proofs, and tests can sometimes turn into proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply severe, probing tests to conjectures (as Polya's severe tests) because they are the most likely to indicate genuine explanatory patterns or generate proof-ideas. Recognize that some tests will lead to new proof-ideas while others expose genuine refutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two patterns of theoretical growth: continuous (piecemeal generalisation) vs critical (alternation of refutation and deeper theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth of knowledge may follow a continuous generalising pattern (piecemeal catching up with heuristic refutations) or an alternation where proofs and refutations produce deeper theoretical shifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating development of theory, note whether progress is mere accumulation of generalisations or critical revolutions where theoretical concept-stretching overtakes naive stretching and produces new explanatory frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and saturation points of deductive guessing
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive guessing and theoretical concept-stretching may reach saturation where no further progress is possible within the current chain; revolutionary new proof-ideas may then be needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to probe for hidden capacities of growth in a theory, but accept that sometimes one must give up on a particular deductive direction and look for new proof-ideas or frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth vs mere increase of content — prefer explanatory depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every increase in content (more general formulas, more cases) constitutes an increase in depth; shallow or trivial generalisation dilutes insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess advances by their explanatory depth and relevance rather than mere extension of scope or producing complicated formulas that add little understanding. Examples: Becker's overcomplicated generalisations are criticized as pretentious trivialities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs and refutations are interdependent (language-dynamics matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refutations and proofs cannot be separated from changes in conceptual, taxonomical, and linguistic frameworks; heuristic activity concerns language-dynamics while logic concerns language-statics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing proofs/refutations, pay attention to how shifts in language or definitions affect the status of statements. Accept that growth of knowledge often entails language-change that cannot be modelled in a single static language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigated concept-stretching may convert mathematical truth into logical truth
rubrics_metrics.description: If one allows arbitrary stretching of constituents of propositions, a proposition that survives all such stretchings becomes 'logically true' (true under all admissible reinterpretations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the danger: either a statement becomes vacuously logically true (immune to refutation only by forbidding meaningful criticism) or meaningless if every stretching is allowed. Evaluate whether claims are being protected into logical truth by over-restricting or over-permitting reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor proofs that explain refutations (explanatory power)
rubrics_metrics.description: A powerful theory or proof is one that not only proves a proposition but explains and integrates the counterexamples/refutations that led to its development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value proofs/theories for their capacity to account for previously anomalous cases (turning counterexamples into examples of a deeper theorem), not merely for formal correctness. Example: test-induced refutations can become the proofs of deeper propositions.
